With the vast positive trend of e-commerce sales, the efficiency of warehouse operations needs to keep pace. Therefore, a part-to-picker warehouse named Robotic Mobile Fulfillment System Warehouse (RMFS) was explicitly designed e-commerce warehouse. This warehouse system can reduce the number of human operators and use robots,  or  in  RMFS,  called  Automated  Guided  Vehicles  (AGV),  to  carry  the  pods. There are several ways to increase the efficiency of the warehouse. This research will focus on the decision problem, SKU to the Pod, or product assignment policy.

This research has three scenarios: SKU to Pod using Random-baseline, Mixed Class, and Mixed Class Affinity policy. ABC classification and association rule using Weighted Support Count is applied to design the second and third scenarios. Then, using a simulation approach, those three scenarios are compared to find the best policy to increase warehouse efficiency. It is indicated by looking at each policy's number of pods transported. The smaller the number of pods, the higher pile-on the SKU to pod policy achieves.

As a result, the last scenario yields the best pile-on with an average number of pods transported of 6.59 pods per order. Meanwhile, the first and second scenarios' results are 7.06 and 6.90, respectively. From that numbers, it can be concluded that the pile-on of the last scenario is 7% and 5% higher than the other two scenarios, even though only 8% of SKUs form the association's rule. This result is verified by using one-way ANOVA.
Keywords:  RMFS,  SKU  to  Pod  Assignment  Policy,  Pile-On,  ABC  Classification, Association Rule

Coronavirus has impacted the entire e-commerce world, changing the nature of business. According to research, 52% of consumers avoid shopping in person and also avoid  crowded  areas.  Furthermore,  36%  avoid  shopping  in  person  until  they  get  a coronavirus vaccine (Bhatti et al., 2020). Therefore, online shopping is one of the most popular  online  activities  worldwide.  In  2020,  retail  e-commerce  sales  worldwide reached US$4.28 trillion, and e-retail revenue is projected to grow to US$6.4 trillion by 2024, as depicted in Figure 1.1 (Chevalier, 2021).

With the growth of e-commerce sales, the efficiency of warehouse operations also needs to keep pace. The Robotic Mobile Fulfillment System (RMFS) warehouse was designed specifically for e-commerce. This warehouse system can reduce the number of human operators and use robots or RMFS, usually called AGV (Automated Guided Vehicles), to carry the shelves, called pods, to the picking stations instead (Merschformann et al., 2019). This type of warehouse can also be categorized as a partto-picker warehouse because the parts, or products, are moved to the picking stations then the operator collects the products(Murray, 2019). In the entire warehouse, order picking  activity  is  usually  the  most  time-consuming  compared  to  others  (Frazelle, 2016). Therefore, increasing the efficiency of order picking also increases warehouse efficiency.

There are several ways to increase the efficiency of the warehouse. It is divided into three levels of decision problems. These are the strategic, tactical, and operational levels  (Merschformann  et  al.,  2019).  Product  assigning  is  a  strategic  decision  that affects order-picking efficiency (Li et al., 2020). Therefore, designing a good policy for product assignment is vital to achieving order-picking efficiency(Silva et al., 2022). Product assigning itself has three decision problems. Those are products (SKU) to pod, pods to zones, and product dispersion over multiple pods(Mirzaei et al., 2022). This research will focus on the first decision problem, products to pod or product assignment policy.

There are three popular product assignment policies which are random, dedicated, and class-based storage assignment policies (Gu et al., 2007). The random assignment policy is clear and straightforward; the SKU randomly assigns the Pod (Mirzaei et al., 2022). On the other hand, a dedicated assignment policy is when each storage location is only used for one particular product. This policy will obtain optimal picking travel distance (Muppani & Adil, 2008). Chan and Chan (2011) had a simulation between random and dedicated assignment policies. The result showed that these policies help to maximize the utilization of storage space and the system throughput, respectively. Using a random instead of dedicated policy might require a smaller warehouse but more  effort  to  track  inventory  accurately  (Gu  et  al.,  2007).  Class-based  storage assignment policy assigns the products after it grouped into classes based on the order frequency (Silva et al., 2022). This policy with two or three classes can achieve the most advantages (Yuan et al., 2018). The two advantages are significant cost savings and space sharing (Mirzaei et al., 2021; Muppani & Adil, 2008).

Other  than  those  three  popular  policies,  there  is  another  policy  for  product assignment  called  the  cluster-based  storage  assignment  policy.  This  policy  clusters correlated items  and then assigns the products into the  Pod based on the cluster to minimize the inventory and material handling cost (Kim, 1993). RMFS warehouses can get advantages from clustering the frequent order together products on the same Pod (Mirzaei et al., 2021). Applying this policy saves order-picking efforts and reduces retrieval time significantly (Frazelle & Sharp, 1989; Mirzaei et al., 2021).

Almost  all  cluster-based  policy  researches  prove  that  storage  assignment  using cluster-based policy is better than other policies based on their objectives. However, none of them are trying to find the best product mixture that could be applied in any other similar cases. The product mixture is the optimal combination of the product classes on pods that minimize the number of pods transported. The fewer pods that need to be transported, which may decrease the number of AGVs needed, the higher pile-on  is  (Merschformann  et  al.,  2019).  Pile-on  is  when  the  pods  offer  most  units necessary to fulfill the orders(Merschformann et al., 2019).

An appropriate product classification also increases order-picking efficiency (Chan &  Chan,  2011).  Generally,  ABC  classification  is  the  most  commonly  used  in warehouse product classification based on order frequency. However, this classification usually solves the second decision problem of product assignment: Pod to zones. Besides, they all use the one-class-one-pod rule, and none try to find the best product class mixture (Products to Pod) for each Pod. Therefore, this research aims to maximize pile-on by finding the best product mixture.

As  e-commerce  has  become  more  prevalent,  researchers  seek  more  efficient methods of managing warehouses and improving picking operations to reduce costs and  inefficiencies  (Galliussi,  2022).  A  robotic  mobile  fulfillment  system  (RMFS) warehouse is a solution for e-commerce sales growth because it fits many SKUs and demands multiple small-quantity orders (Azadeh et al., 2019). In addition, this type of warehouse is introduced as a solution for automated storage/retrieval system (AS/RS) warehouse problems which are the rigidity of changing inventory locations, the high cost of setup, and manual re-slotting (Enright & Wurman, 2011; Wurman et al., 2008).

The  solution  offered  by  RMFS  is  robots  that  carry  pods  on  the  conventional warehouse called shelves, with items on the pods (Enright  & Wurman, 2011). The robots carry one Pod for each robot from storage locations to replenishment or picking stations for later the pods being filled or picked by the workers (Kim et al., 2020). Each picking station receives a customer order when it arrives. Then pods containing items in  the  order  are  transported  to  the  station  by  robots.  The  operators  remain  at  their stations because all items are carried by robots (Enright & Wurman, 2011). The RMFS layout  is  commonly  arranged  with  storage  zones  of  inventory  pods,  replenishment stations, and picking stations. The illustration can be seen in Figure 2.1.

There  are  several  benefits  of  the  RMFS  warehouse.  In  2016,  it  was  found  that RMFS's throughput is higher than AS/RS depending on the number of AGVs and SKUs (Beuters et al., 2016). The throughput increases when the inventory is dispersed into multiple  pods,  the  warehouse  has  an  optimal  number  of  stations,  and  the  pods  are replenished before empty Tessensohn et al. (2020). The other benefit is that the system can quickly adapt to new replenishment policies, and even if a robot breaks down, it will not affect productivity significantly (Enright & Wurman, 2011).

The  study  conducted  by  Yang  (2022)  evaluated  two  association  rule  mining methods:  the  Jaccard  Index  and  the  Weighted  Support  Count  (WSC).  The  Jaccard Index, developed by Swiss mathematician Paul Jaccard, is a well-known measure of similarity between sets that considers their similarities and differences. This method has been widely used in various fields, including information retrieval and data mining, to quantify the similarity between different sets of items. The study also employs the Jaccard Index to measure the association between goods in a storage assignment study.

On  the  other  hand,  the  Weighted  Support  Count  (WSC),  which  represents  the relationship between any pair of goods, incorporates the concepts of support and lift developed  by  Ming-Huang  Chiang  et  al.  (2014).  The  study  results  show  that  the Weighted  Support  Count  outperforms  the  Jaccard  Index  in  terms  of  accuracy  and effectiveness, as Yang (2022) demonstrated. This comparative study provides valuable insights into selecting the most appropriate method for a specific data analysis problem and contributes to the ongoing research in association rule mining.

elements.text: Following the generation of new data orders, the subsequent step in the research process is the comprehensive analysis of inventory. This stage comprises two essential sub-processes,  namely,  SKU  classification  and  the  determination  of  the  number  of slots. SKU classification is a crucial component of inventory analysis, as it provides a clear  understanding  of  the  types  of  products  in  stock.  In  addition,  by  categorizing products into distinct groups, the researcher can analyze the stock more effectively and make informed decisions regarding inventory management.

Determining the number of slots in Pods is  another  crucial  aspect  of  inventory analysis. This process involves calculating the number of storage spaces required for each  SKU  in  the  Pod  system  to  ensure  that  the  inventory  remains  organized  and efficiently managed.

The SKU classification in this stage is performed by dividing the SKUs into three distinct classes based on their order frequency. The ABC rule is used, which results in 10%,  30%,  and  60%  of  the  total  SKUs  being  classified  as  class  A,  B,  and  C, respectively.

Therefore, class A SKUs account for 60% of the cumulative order frequency, class B SKUs account for 25%, and class C SKUs account for 15%. The Pareto chart of the ABC classification  can  be  seen  in  Figure  3.2.  This  classification  provides  a  visual representation of the relative importance of each SKU class and serves as a guide for inventory management decisions.

The SKU-to-Pod assignment in this study process is carried out in three distinct scenarios: random, mixed-class, and mixed-class affinity. The following sub-sections provide a comprehensive explanation of each scenario and its characteristics.

In  the  random  scenario  of  the  SKU-to-Pod  assignment  process,  the  SKUs  are assigned to Pods randomly, taking into account the data order and inventory analysis conducted in the preceding step. However, it should be noted that this scenario operates within a set of guidelines, specifically that each SKU is dispersed across several Pods.

This random scenario acts as a baseline for comparison with the other scenarios, serving  as  a  starting  point  for  further  analysis.  The  results  of  the  random  scenario provide a foundation for determining the impact of different approaches to the SKUto-Pod assignment process

The mixed-class assignment scenario requires the completion of three key steps. Firstly,  the  product  mixture  percentage  must  be  calculated  using  the  principles  of Independent Event probability as described in Equations (2) and (3). As per Shafer (1996),  independent  events  do  not  depend  on  one  another  for  their  occurrence. Therefore, this calculation determines the appropriate number of Pods for each class combination,  as  the  orders  between  classes  are  not  interdependent.  Thus,  the independent  event  probability  is  used  to  establish  the  probability  of  each  product mixture. In the second step, the SKU to Pod ratio must be calculated using Equation (4) to determine the number of slots required for each class assigned to a given Pod. Lastly, the SKUs are assigned based on their respective class.

The results of these three steps provide a comprehensive analysis of the mixedclass  assignment  scenario,  allowing  for  a  thorough  evaluation  of  the  impact  of prioritizing high-frequency SKUs on the efficiency of the Pod system. Furthermore, the  findings  will  inform  decisions  regarding  the  assignment  of  SKUs  to  Pods  and optimize the utilization of the Pod system.

In the final SKU to pod assignment scenario, the process is an improvement over the previous mixed-class scenario. In  order  to  establish  the  validity  of  the  simulation,  it  is  imperative  to  perform statistical tests. The replication adequacy test is the initial step, which assesses whether the number of replications is sufficient to produce reliable results. Subsequently, an Analysis of Variance (ANOVA) is conducted to validate the significant differences between the scenarios through a hypothesis test. These tests are critical to ensure the accuracy and credibility of the simulation results.

The replication adequacy test utilizes Equations (8) and (9) as its mathematical formula, as described by Harrel et al. (2012). Therefore, this test is crucial in ensuring that  the  replications  conducted  in  the  simulation  are  sufficient  to  produce  accurate results.

This type of ANOVA addresses a simulation that  has  solely  one  factor.  In  this  research,  one  factor  is  the  policy  of  SKU  to  pod assignment. In this study, we created a sample of the 55000 actual data order by generating a 10000-data order. This step was crucial in ensuring that the simulation results reflected reality as closely as possible. In addition, the generated data was intended to provide a representative picture of the actual data.

To examine the distribution  patterns  of  both  the  generated  and  actual  data,  the researchers  employed  @RISK,  a  commonly  used  software  for  risk  analysis.  The analysis  showed  that  both  the  generated  and  actual  data  exhibited  a  lognormal distribution. This analysis was depicted in Figures 4.1 and 4.2, which displayed the distribution of both data sets. The similarities in the distribution patterns of both data sets indicated that the generated data successfully represented the actual data.

Based on the total frequency of orders, the 5000 SKUs can be classified into ABC classes. 10% of SKUs, which is 500 SKUs, that dominate 60% of total order frequency are  categorized  into  class  A. Moreover,  the  SKUs  that  are  minor contributors to the total order frequency are classified into class C.

Different from determining ABC classification, the number of slots per SKU is based on the quantity of order, not the frequency. Therefore, each class has different slots depending on their order quantity. Then, to define the number of slots, Equation (1) is used. The calculation below shows how to determine the number of slots given that the confidence level is 95%, which the Z score can be seen in Appendix 1, and the slot  capacity  is  ten  units.  The  slot  capacity  is  assumed  to  be  ten  units  because  the average number of units ordered per SKU is five, and more than 96% of the SKUs are ordered in less than ten units on each order. With this assumption, the replenishment number of each Pod will vary. Pods containing class C most likely have the highest number of replenishments, and pods containing class A have the lowest number of replenishments.

The calculation shows that even though class A has the smallest number of SKUs with 500, its number of slots is the largest with 106 slots/SKU. elements.text: In this study, 5000 SKUs were categorized into three classes: A, B, and C. The first 500 SKUs were classified as Class A, the following 1500 SKUs as Class B, and the remaining  3000  SKUs  as  Class  C.  These  classifications  were  made  based  on predetermined criteria.

We randomly assigned the 5000 into 935 pods to ensure a balanced distribution of SKUs. This random assignment aimed to prevent the clustering of similar SKUs and promote a more even distribution throughout the warehouse. The 935 pods served as storage units for the 5000 SKUs, allowing for efficient organization and retrieval of items in the warehouse.

In this scenario, we analyzed 10000 orders and found that 9304 orders contained SKUs from Class A, while 7548 and 4627 orders contained SKUs from Class B and Class C, respectively. To determine the likelihood of orders containing each class, the researchers divided the total orders of each class by the total number of orders.

Having established the probability of orders containing each class, we then defined the  mixed-class  order  probability  using  Equation  (2).  This  probability  was  then converted into the product mixture percentage in the warehouse. Table 4.4 summarizes the probability of mixed-class orders and the corresponding number of pods required for each mixture. This information can help determine the optimal storage arrangements for the warehouse to ensure efficient order picking and minimize the risk of stock shortages.

The highest probability is the mixture of class A and class B orders by 37.7%. From that  percentage,  the  pods  needed  for  AB  pod  is  352  pods.  The  second  highest probability is the mixture of all three classes by 32.5% or equal to 306 pods. Then it was followed by only A pod and AC pod, with 116 and 100 pods needed, respectively. Finally, the three lowest are only B pod, BC mixture pod, and only C pod with less than 3% each.

After  determining  the  number  of  pods  for  each  mixture,  the  next  one  to  be determined is the number of slots for each class on every Pod using Equation (4). Table 4.5 depicts the percentage of slots in each class. It can be seen that class A will always dominate more than 50% of every Pod's product mixture, which are the ABC, AB, and AC pod. Class B dominates approximately a third of the ABC and AB pod and two third of the BC pod. On the other hand, class C contributes the smallest percentage of every  Pod's  product  mixture  by  16%,  22%,  and  37%  for  ABC,  AC,  and  BC  pods, respectively. With 100 slots per pod capacity, the number of slots of each class on each product mixture pod will be easily defined. That shows in Table 4.6. Then the SKUs are assigned randomly based on the number of slot rules.

To  do  this  scenario,  the  first  two  steps,  determining  product  mixture  and  slots percentage, are the same as the second. The difference is how the SKU is assigned to the Pod. The rules must be found in this scenario using association analysis with the Google Colab tool. The result is only 8% of SKUs or equal to 400 SKUs that form the rules.

Meanwhile, no rules were formed for most of the SKUs in Class B and C because the frequency of those SKUs ordered together is too low. Therefore, the 400 SKUs must be assigned close to each other while the rest are assigned randomly.

By running the simulation based on the flowcharts in Figures 3.5 and 3.6, the output of the simulation is excel data. The output data has the same format as the data order shown in Table 3.1. From the output, the number of pods transported for the whole order can be defined by calculating the total number of pods assigned to each order based on order_dum and pod_id data. Therefore, the performance indicator used for the simulation result is the average number of pods transported for 10000 orders can be calculated. The lower the average, the higher the pile-on achieved.

Figure 4.3 shows the simulation result for the random assignment scenario. It can be seen that within ten replications, the result is not very similar. With a random SKUto-pod assignment policy, the average simulation result ranges from 6.92 to 7.21 and averages 7.08.

Table 4.7 compares each scenario from replication one to ten. It can be seen that the last scene has the best result, which is the lowest average of pods transported. The mixed  affinity  scenario  increases  the  baseline  scenario  by  6.4%,  while  the  mixed scenario only increases the baseline result by 3.49%.

The result shows that ABC classification in SKU to pod assignment policy affects the number of pods transported. For example, scenario 1, or the baseline scenario, with random policy, has the highest average number of pods transported because the SKUs are too dispersed in multiple pods without rules. This result makes the required pods more than other policies in SKU to pod assignment. Meanwhile, the simulation result proves that applying ABC classification on the second and third scenarios yields better warehouse performance.

With only 8% or more than 400 SKUs forming the association rules, it might seem impossible  for  the  third  scenario  to  achieve  the  best  simulation  result,  especially compared to the second scenario. Because the second and third scenario is similar, and the  difference  is  only  the  use  of  association  rules  in  the  third  one.  However,  after reviewing the order data, it was found that those 400 SKUs dominated 55% of the total order. Therefore, even though not even a tenth of the total SKUs are associated with each other, it still significantly affects the pile-on if those SKUs dominate the total order.

Furthermore, referring to the simulation results and analysis above, it can be said that choosing the suitable SKU for the pod assignment policy can affect warehouse performance. Compared to random and mixed class policy, mixed class affinity policy is the best to maximize pile-on. It can also be implemented in an actual e-commerce warehouse, considering that in that type of warehouse, a high pile-on is required due to the high number of orders and a wide variety of SKUs in each order to increase the warehouse's efficiency. With notes, there are associations between SKUs, and those SKUs dominate the total orders.

After getting the simulation result, the next thing to do is check whether the number of replication is sufficient. If it is insufficient, then the simulation needs to be replicated more. On the other hand, if it is already sufficient, then the result is verified using OneWay ANOVA.

Due to limited time, there are only ten replications completed. Therefore, to prove that the ten replications are enough, the replications adequacy test must be done using Equation (8). The value of t and Z can be found on the Students T distribution table in Appendix 2 and Z table in Appendix 1, given that the confidence level is 95%.

With  the  mean  and  standard  deviation  of  the  simulation  result,  the  replications needed are at least eight times those. Therefore, the ten replications done are sufficient for this research.

The simulation results must be validated to ensure their reliability and accuracy. This  validation  process  involves  performing  a  one-way  ANOVA  after  ensuring  an adequate  number  of  replications.  The  hypothesis  test,  shown  in  Figure  4.6,  is  the foundation for this validation.

A one-way factor ANOVA is a statistical technique used to determine if there are significant  differences  between  the  means  of  three  or  more  groups.  The  groups  are referred to as "scenarios." The goal of the ANOVA test is to establish if the differences in the simulation results of the three scenarios are statistically significant or if they may have occurred by chance.

The p-value, which measures the strength of evidence against the null hypothesis, is an important factor in the hypothesis test. The null hypothesis assumes that there are no significant differences between the scenarios. A p-value of less than 0.05 is widely accepted as statistically significant, meaning there is less than a 5% probability that the results could have occurred by chance.

In  this  instance,  the  p-value  of  0.000000182  is  significantly  less  than  0.05, indicating strong evidence against the null hypothesis. As a result, we can reject the null hypothesis and conclude that the three scenarios are significantly different.

There are several ways to increase the efficiency of the RMFS warehouse. One of the decision problems is the SKU to Pod assignment policy. Although the different policy makes different warehouse performances, the policy with the lowest number of transported  pods  is  the  best  to  achieve  the  highest  pile-on  in  the  warehouse.  This research tests three policies as a scenario: Random-baseline, Mixed class, and Mixed Class Affinity policy. Each policy has a different rule for its product mixture.

The simulation result shows that the last scenario yields the best pile-on with an average number of pods transported of 6.63 pods per order. Meanwhile, the first and second scenarios' results are 7.08 and 6.84, respectively. From that numbers, it can be concluded that the pile-on of the last scenario is 6.4% and 3.02% higher than the other two scenarios, even though only 8% of SKUs form the association's rule. However, it must be highlighted that 8% of SKUs dominate 55% of the order data.

The  result  is  verified  by  using  one-way  ANOVA.  The  p-value  for  the  three scenarios is less than 0.05, which means those scenarios are significantly different. Therefore, it can be concluded that the SKU-to-pod scenarios have affected the RMFS warehouse's efficiency. The mixed-class affinity policy is verified as the best compared to random and mixed-class policies.

Before deciding  what the best SKU  to  Pod  assignment  policy  to be implemented in the actual warehouse is, things need to be considered the most: the number of SKUs that associate with each other and the contribution of these SKUs to the  total  order.  Suppose  the  contribution  of  associated  SKUs  is  high.  In  that  case, implementing the Mixed Class Affinity assignment policy might fit better than other policies to maximize pile-on.

For future research, there are still many things for the RMFS warehouse that need to be researched deeper. For example, from the side of product mixture in SKU to Pod, considering  the  quantities  and  dimensions  of  each  SKU  can  be  the  next  research opportunity. Because in this research, both things are made uniform. At the same time, quantities and dimensions should affect the SKU to pod assignment.

With the vast positive trend of e-commerce sales, the efficiency of warehouse operations needs to keep pace. Therefore, a part-to-picker warehouse named Robotic Mobile Fulfillment System Warehouse (RMFS) was explicitly designed e-commerce warehouse. This warehouse system can reduce the number of human operators and use robots,  or  in  RMFS,  called  Automated  Guided  Vehicles  (AGV),  to  carry  the  pods. There are several ways to increase the efficiency of the warehouse. This research will focus on the decision problem, SKU to the Pod, or product assignment policy.
This research has three scenarios: SKU to Pod using Random-baseline, Mixed Class, and Mixed Class Affinity policy. ABC classification and association rule using Weighted Support Count is applied to design the second and third scenarios. Then, using a simulation approach, those three scenarios are compared to find the best policy to increase warehouse efficiency. It is indicated by looking at each policy's number of pods transported. The smaller the number of pods, the higher pile-on the SKU to pod policy achieves.

As a result, the last scenario yields the best pile-on with an average number of pods transported of 6.59 pods per order. Meanwhile, the first and second scenarios' results are 7.06 and 6.90, respectively. From that numbers, it can be concluded that the pile-on of the last scenario is 7% and 5% higher than the other two scenarios, even though only 8% of SKUs form the association's rule. This result is verified by using one-way ANOVA.
Keywords:  RMFS,  SKU  to  Pod  Assignment  Policy,  Pile-On,  ABC  Classification, Association Rule

Coronavirus has impacted the entire e-commerce world, changing the nature of business. According to research, 52% of consumers avoid shopping in person and also avoid  crowded  areas.  Furthermore,  36%  avoid  shopping  in  person  until  they  get  a coronavirus vaccine (Bhatti et al., 2020). Therefore, online shopping is one of the most popular  online  activities  worldwide.  In  2020,  retail  e-commerce  sales  worldwide reached US$4.28 trillion, and e-retail revenue is projected to grow to US$6.4 trillion by 2024, as depicted in Figure 1.1 (Chevalier, 2021).

With the growth of e-commerce sales, the efficiency of warehouse operations also needs to keep pace. The Robotic Mobile Fulfillment System (RMFS) warehouse was designed specifically for e-commerce. This warehouse system can reduce the number of human operators and use robots or RMFS, usually called AGV (Automated Guided Vehicles), to carry the shelves, called pods, to the picking stations instead (Merschformann et al., 2019). This type of warehouse can also be categorized as a partto-picker warehouse because the parts, or products, are moved to the picking stations then the operator collects the products(Murray, 2019). In the entire warehouse, order picking  activity  is  usually  the  most  time-consuming  compared  to  others  (Frazelle, 2016). Therefore, increasing the efficiency of order picking also increases warehouse efficiency.

There are several ways to increase the efficiency of the warehouse. It is divided into three levels of decision problems. These are the strategic, tactical, and operational levels  (Merschformann  et  al.,  2019).  Product  assigning  is  a  strategic  decision  that affects order-picking efficiency (Li et al., 2020). Therefore, designing a good policy for product assignment is vital to achieving order-picking efficiency(Silva et al., 2022). Product assigning itself has three decision problems. Those are products (SKU) to pod, pods to zones, and product dispersion over multiple pods(Mirzaei et al., 2022). This research will focus on the first decision problem, products to pod or product assignment policy.

There are three popular product assignment policies which are random, dedicated, and class-based storage assignment policies (Gu et al., 2007). The random assignment policy is clear and straightforward; the SKU randomly assigns the Pod (Mirzaei et al., 2022). On the other hand, a dedicated assignment policy is when each storage location is only used for one particular product. This policy will obtain optimal picking travel distance (Muppani & Adil, 2008). Chan and Chan (2011) had a simulation between random and dedicated assignment policies. The result showed that these policies help to maximize the utilization of storage space and the system throughput, respectively. Using a random instead of dedicated policy might require a smaller warehouse but more  effort  to  track  inventory  accurately  (Gu  et  al.,  2007).  Class-based  storage assignment policy assigns the products after it grouped into classes based on the order frequency (Silva et al., 2022). This policy with two or three classes can achieve the most advantages (Yuan et al., 2018). The two advantages are significant cost savings and space sharing (Mirzaei et al., 2021; Muppani & Adil, 2008).

Other  than  those  three  popular  policies,  there  is  another  policy  for  product assignment  called  the  cluster-based  storage  assignment  policy.  This  policy  clusters correlated items  and then assigns the products into the  Pod based on the cluster to minimize the inventory and material handling cost (Kim, 1993). RMFS warehouses can get advantages from clustering the frequent order together products on the same Pod (Mirzaei et al., 2021). Applying this policy saves order-picking efforts and reduces retrieval time significantly (Frazelle & Sharp, 1989; Mirzaei et al., 2021).
Almost  all  cluster-based  policy  researches  prove  that  storage  assignment  using cluster-based policy is better than other policies based on their objectives. However, none of them are trying to find the best product mixture that could be applied in any other similar cases. The product mixture is the optimal combination of the product classes on pods that minimize the number of pods transported. The fewer pods that need to be transported, which may decrease the number of AGVs needed, the higher pile-on  is  (Merschformann  et  al.,  2019).  Pile-on  is  when  the  pods  offer  most  units necessary to fulfill the orders(Merschformann et al., 2019).

An appropriate product classification also increases order-picking efficiency (Chan &  Chan,  2011).  Generally,  ABC  classification  is  the  most  commonly  used  in warehouse product classification based on order frequency. However, this classification usually solves the second decision problem of product assignment: Pod to zones. Besides, they all use the one-class-one-pod rule, and none try to find the best product class mixture (Products to Pod) for each Pod. Therefore, this research aims to maximize pile-on by finding the best product mixture.

Based on the background previously described, the objectives of this research can be described as follows:
1. To determine the optimal product mixture percentage within the warehouse by analyzing the various factors influencing warehouse space utilization.
2. To establish the best policy for the SKU to pod decision problem by employing a simulation-based approach. This objective aims to determine the most suitable and  effective strategy for allocating products  to specific storage  pods, considering various constraints such as demand patterns, inventory levels, and available space. Furthermore, the simulation approach will enable us to analyze the performance of different strategies and determine the one that offers the best results.

The following limitations of the research must be acknowledged:
3. The  AGVs  utilized  in  the  research  are  capable  of  picking  and  replenishing activities. However, this does not consider the possibility of specialization of AGVs  for  specific  tasks,  which  may  result  in  improved  efficiency  and productivity.
4. The assumption in this research is that the pods will be directly replenished as soon as they become empty, thus ensuring that sufficient quantities of products are always available to fulfill customer orders.
5. The  dimensions  of  the  SKUs  are  assumed  to  be  uniform  in  this  research. However, this may result in a simplified model that may not accurately reflect the diversity and complexity of real-world scenarios, where the dimensions and shapes of products may vary significantly.
6. The scope of this research is limited to the replenishment aspect of warehouse operations and does not consider the order-picking process. This means that the overall efficiency and productivity of the warehouse are not considered in this study.
It is important to acknowledge these limitations to understand the research findings' limitations  and  the  extent  to  which  they  can  be  applied  in  real-world  scenarios. Nevertheless,  the  results  of  this  research  still  provide  valuable  insights  into  the optimization of warehouse operations and may inform future studies in this area.

As  e-commerce  has  become  more  prevalent,  researchers  seek  more  efficient methods of managing warehouses and improving picking operations to reduce costs and  inefficiencies  (Galliussi,  2022).  A  robotic  mobile  fulfillment  system  (RMFS) warehouse is a solution for e-commerce sales growth because it fits many SKUs and demands multiple small-quantity orders (Azadeh et al., 2019). In addition, this type of warehouse is introduced as a solution for automated storage/retrieval system (AS/RS) warehouse problems which are the rigidity of changing inventory locations, the high cost of setup, and manual re-slotting (Enright & Wurman, 2011; Wurman et al., 2008).

The  solution  offered  by  RMFS  is  robots  that  carry  pods  on  the  conventional warehouse called shelves, with items on the pods (Enright  & Wurman, 2011). The robots carry one Pod for each robot from storage locations to replenishment or picking stations for later the pods being filled or picked by the workers (Kim et al., 2020). Each picking station receives a customer order when it arrives. Then pods containing items in  the  order  are  transported  to  the  station  by  robots.  The  operators  remain  at  their stations because all items are carried by robots (Enright & Wurman, 2011). The RMFS layout  is  commonly  arranged  with  storage  zones  of  inventory  pods,  replenishment stations, and picking stations. The illustration can be seen in Figure 2.1.

There  are  several  benefits  of  the  RMFS  warehouse.  In  2016,  it  was  found  that RMFS's throughput is higher than AS/RS depending on the number of AGVs and SKUs (Beuters et al., 2016). The throughput increases when the inventory is dispersed into multiple  pods,  the  warehouse  has  an  optimal  number  of  stations,  and  the  pods  are replenished before empty Tessensohn et al. (2020). The other benefit is that the system can quickly adapt to new replenishment policies, and even if a robot breaks down, it will not affect productivity significantly (Enright & Wurman, 2011).

The  study  conducted  by  Yang  (2022)  evaluated  two  association  rule  mining methods:  the  Jaccard  Index  and  the  Weighted  Support  Count  (WSC).  The  Jaccard Index, developed by Swiss mathematician Paul Jaccard, is a well-known measure of similarity between sets that considers their similarities and differences. This method has been widely used in various fields, including information retrieval and data mining, to quantify the similarity between different sets of items. The study also employs the Jaccard Index to measure the association between goods in a storage assignment study.
On  the  other  hand,  the  Weighted  Support  Count  (WSC),  which  represents  the relationship between any pair of goods, incorporates the concepts of support and lift developed  by  Ming-Huang  Chiang  et  al.  (2014).  The  study  results  show  that  the Weighted  Support  Count  outperforms  the  Jaccard  Index  in  terms  of  accuracy  and effectiveness, as Yang (2022) demonstrated. This comparative study provides valuable insights into selecting the most appropriate method for a specific data analysis problem and contributes to the ongoing research in association rule mining.

Following the generation of new data orders, the subsequent step in the research process is the comprehensive analysis of inventory. This stage comprises two essential sub-processes,  namely,  SKU  classification  and  the  determination  of  the  number  of slots. SKU classification is a crucial component of inventory analysis, as it provides a clear  understanding  of  the  types  of  products  in  stock.  In  addition,  by  categorizing products into distinct groups, the researcher can analyze the stock more effectively and make informed decisions regarding inventory management.
Determining the number of slots in Pods is  another  crucial  aspect  of  inventory analysis. This process involves calculating the number of storage spaces required for each  SKU  in  the  Pod  system  to  ensure  that  the  inventory  remains  organized  and efficiently managed.

The SKU classification in this stage is performed by dividing the SKUs into three distinct classes based on their order frequency. The ABC rule is used, which results in 10%,  30%,  and  60%  of  the  total  SKUs  being  classified  as  class  A,  B,  and  C, respectively.
Therefore, class A SKUs account for 60% of the cumulative order frequency, class B SKUs account for 25%, and class C SKUs account for 15%. The Pareto chart of the ABC classification  can  be  seen  in  Figure  3.2.  This  classification  provides  a  visual representation of the relative importance of each SKU class and serves as a guide for inventory management decisions.

The SKU-to-Pod assignment in this study process is carried out in three distinct scenarios: random, mixed-class, and mixed-class affinity. The following sub-sections provide a comprehensive explanation of each scenario and its characteristics.

In  the  random  scenario  of  the  SKU-to-Pod  assignment  process,  the  SKUs  are assigned to Pods randomly, taking into account the data order and inventory analysis conducted in the preceding step. However, it should be noted that this scenario operates within a set of guidelines, specifically that each SKU is dispersed across several Pods.
This random scenario acts as a baseline for comparison with the other scenarios, serving  as  a  starting  point  for  further  analysis.  The  results  of  the  random  scenario provide a foundation for determining the impact of different approaches to the SKUto-Pod assignment process

The mixed-class assignment scenario requires the completion of three key steps. Firstly,  the  product  mixture  percentage  must  be  calculated  using  the  principles  of Independent Event probability as described in Equations (2) and (3). As per Shafer (1996),  independent  events  do  not  depend  on  one  another  for  their  occurrence. Therefore, this calculation determines the appropriate number of Pods for each class combination,  as  the  orders  between  classes  are  not  interdependent.  Thus,  the independent  event  probability  is  used  to  establish  the  probability  of  each  product mixture. In the second step, the SKU to Pod ratio must be calculated using Equation (4) to determine the number of slots required for each class assigned to a given Pod. Lastly, the SKUs are assigned based on their respective class.
The results of these three steps provide a comprehensive analysis of the mixedclass  assignment  scenario,  allowing  for  a  thorough  evaluation  of  the  impact  of prioritizing high-frequency SKUs on the efficiency of the Pod system. Furthermore, the  findings  will  inform  decisions  regarding  the  assignment  of  SKUs  to  Pods  and optimize the utilization of the Pod system.

In the final SKU to pod assignment scenario, the process is an improvement over the previous mixed-class scenario. The first two steps, calculating the product mixture percentage  and  the  SKU  in  pod  ratio,  are  similar  to  the  mixed-class  scenario.  The crucial difference lies in assigning SKUs to the Pod, which occurs based on the affinity between the items, as inferred from the order data history.
Classifying SKUs before the association analysis is imperative, as numerous SKUs in the e-commerce warehouse can make the analysis challenging. By classifying the SKUs, the association rules analysis is streamlined, hence the need to complete the classification before the association analysis. After finished the association analysis, the last step is assigning SKUs to the pods based on the first two steps. In this last step, there are several procedures to assign the SKU, those are:

1. Assign the highest frequent SKUs on the highest percentage product mixture,
2. Assign SKUs with the highest affinity with the assigned SKUs,
3. Assign  the  next  highest  affinity  SKUs  of  the  next  highest  frequent  SKUs assigned,
4. Assign SKUs for the following product mixture.

In this study, the simulation of the three SKU-to-Pod assignment scenarios will be conducted using the NetLogo software. The simulation will generate the number of pods  visited  for  each  scenario  to  evaluate  the  efficiency  of  the  scenarios.  This evaluation will be based on the number of pods visited and comparing them with the other two scenarios. The objective is to determine which scenario produces the highest pile and hence, the most efficient storage allocation of the SKUs in the Pod system.

The design of the warehouse simulation in NetLogo is depicted in Figure 3.4. The simulation consists of three distinct sections: the picking station, the storage area, and the replenishment station. First, the picker awaits the arrival of AGVs carrying pods at the picking station. Next, the storage area is where the pods are stored, ready to be carried by AGVs. Finally, the replenishment station is where empty pods are refilled, ensuring that the storage area remains fully stocked. The following are the key elements found in the storage area of the warehouse in NetLogo:
1. Pod: A container where items are stored.
2. Selected  Pod:  A  Pod  that  has  been  chosen  and  matches  the  items  with  the assigned orders.
3. AGV (Automated Guided Vehicle): A robot responsible for transporting pods to the picking and replenishment station.
4. Aisle: The designated path for AGV to move and access pods in the storage area.
5. Empty Storage Location: An available space in the storage area where pods can be stored.

The simulation results must be validated to ensure their reliability and accuracy. This  validation  process  involves  performing  a  one-way  ANOVA  after  ensuring  an adequate  number  of  replications.  The  hypothesis  test,  shown  in  Figure  4.6,  is  the foundation for this validation.
A one-way factor ANOVA is a statistical technique used to determine if there are significant  differences  between  the  means  of  three  or  more  groups.  The  groups  are referred to as "scenarios." The goal of the ANOVA test is to establish if the differences in the simulation results of the three scenarios are statistically significant or if they may have occurred by chance.
The p-value, which measures the strength of evidence against the null hypothesis, is an important factor in the hypothesis test. The null hypothesis assumes that there are no significant differences between the scenarios. A p-value of less than 0.05 is widely accepted as statistically significant, meaning there is less than a 5% probability that the results could have occurred by chance.

In  this  instance,  the  p-value  of  0.000000182  is  significantly  less  than  0.05, indicating strong evidence against the null hypothesis. As a result, we can reject the null hypothesis and conclude that the three scenarios are significantly different.

There are several ways to increase the efficiency of the RMFS warehouse. One of the decision problems is the SKU to Pod assignment policy. Although the different policy makes different warehouse performances, the policy with the lowest number of transported  pods  is  the  best  to  achieve  the  highest  pile-on  in  the  warehouse.  This research tests three policies as a scenario: Random-baseline, Mixed class, and Mixed Class Affinity policy. Each policy has a different rule for its product mixture.
The simulation result shows that the last scenario yields the best pile-on with an average number of pods transported of 6.63 pods per order. Meanwhile, the first and second scenarios' results are 7.08 and 6.84, respectively. From that numbers, it can be concluded that the pile-on of the last scenario is 6.4% and 3.02% higher than the other two scenarios, even though only 8% of SKUs form the association's rule. However, it must be highlighted that 8% of SKUs dominate 55% of the order data.

The  result  is  verified  by  using  one-way  ANOVA.  The  p-value  for  the  three scenarios is less than 0.05, which means those scenarios are significantly different. Therefore, it can be concluded that the SKU-to-pod scenarios have affected the RMFS warehouse's efficiency. The mixed-class affinity policy is verified as the best compared to random and mixed-class policies.

Before deciding  what the best SKU  to  Pod  assignment  policy  to be implemented in the actual warehouse is, things need to be considered the most: the number of SKUs that associate with each other and the contribution of these SKUs to the  total  order.  Suppose  the  contribution  of  associated  SKUs  is  high.  In  that  case, implementing the Mixed Class Affinity assignment policy might fit better than other policies to maximize pile-on.

For future research, there are still many things for the RMFS warehouse that need to be researched deeper. For example, from the side of product mixture in SKU to Pod, considering  the  quantities  and  dimensions  of  each  SKU  can  be  the  next  research opportunity. Because in this research, both things are made uniform. At the same time, quantities and dimensions should affect the SKU to pod assignment.
